repo.description:
## Summary

Portainer makes outbound network requests on a user's behalf in several features: cloning Git repositories for stacks, custom templates, edge stacks and file previews; fetching Helm repository indexes and charts; pinging container registries; retrieving application templates and Kubernetes manifests from a URL; proxying GitLab API calls; and contacting an OAuth provider. In each of these the destination was taken from user- or admin-supplied input and used to open a server-side connection while validating only the URL's syntax, not the address it resolved to. An authenticated user who can reach one of these features - several are available to the lowest-privilege standard role - could cause the Portainer server to connect to hosts the user could not reach directly, including internal services and cloud instance-metadata endpoints.

Portainer is a self-hosted management plane, and the reach of these requests is bounded by where the operator deploys it and how the surrounding network is segmented. Under Portainer's [shared-responsibility model](https://docs.portainer.io/advanced/security), the operator owns network exposure, egress control and segmentation of the server; Portainer owns the controls that decide who may reach a feature.

Portainer has introduced a centralized destination allow-list covering these outbound paths, together with an SSRF mode offering `Audit` and `Enforce` that deployers may choose to use. It is opt-in and ships disabled, because Portainer deployments routinely make legitimate outbound requests to internal Git servers, registries and Helm repositories that an unconditional private-range block would break - the destination policy is one only the operator can author. The mode is a Business Edition control; Community Edition ships the same code but has no way to enable it, so on Community Edition the server's outbound reach is governed by the operator's network posture (see Affected Versions).

This is a single class of issue - Server-Side Request Forgery (CWE-918) - reported independently against many endpoints by a number of researchers over several months. This advisory consolidates those reports and describes the centralized control that addresses them.

## Severity

**Medium**

Exploitation needs no user interaction and little sophistication, but it does require an authenticated account: the Git file-preview, Git-backed stack and template creation, registry ping and Helm repository endpoints are reachable by any authenticated user, while the application-template URL and the OAuth resource URI are admin-configured. The direct impact on Portainer itself is limited - these vectors do not compromise Portainer's own integrity or availability, and the confidentiality loss on Portainer's own data is marginal. The meaningful impact falls on *subsequent* systems the server can reach, and how far that reaches is governed by posture the operator owns: network exposure, segmentation and egress filtering, together with whether the SSRF mode has been audited and enforced. Worst-case outcomes - reading a cloud instance-metadata credential, and the full-read and OAuth-token-forwarding sub-vectors - depend on the server having unrestricted reach to those endpoints, and a deployment following the hardening guidance constrains them. Because the impact that remains is bounded by deployer-owned configuration rather than by the failure of a Portainer control that was in force, the class is rated Medium rather than High.

## Affected Versions

These vectors have been present across most of the product's history. The issue is not tied to a single recently-introduced feature.

Portainer Community Edition and Portainer Business Edition share release version numbering; the table below applies to both editions.

The centralized outbound-destination protections cover every path named in this advisory from the following release:

| Branch                | First vulnerable | Fixed in   |
|-----------------------|------------------|------------|
| 2.39.x (LTS)          | 2.39.0           | see below  |
| 2.40.x - 2.44.x (STS) | all prior        | see below  |
| 2.45.x (LTS)          | 2.45.0           | **2.45.1** |

**2.45.1 is the release to upgrade to, from any earlier version.** Protections were added incrementally from 2.39.6 and 2.43.0 onward, but the paths named in this advisory are only all covered from 2.45.1. Earlier releases on the 2.39.x and 2.40.x - 2.44.x lines carry partial coverage and will not receive further work on this class: the 2.40.x - 2.44.x short-term-support lines reached end of life with the release of 2.45.0, and the 2.39.x LTS line is receiving no further changes in this area. Operators on those lines should upgrade to 2.45.1 and apply the deployment measures below in the meantime.

Portainer releases prior to 2.39 are end-of-life and will not receive a fix.

### Community Edition

Portainer's responsibility under the [shared-responsibility model](https://docs.portainer.io/advanced/security) is that the controls it ships work as documented. The SSRF mode is a Business Edition control. Community Edition ships the same code paths but provides no supported way to enable the mode on any release, so Community Edition has no in-product control over the destinations the server may reach, and that reach is the deployer's responsibility: network segmentation and egress filtering, per the Workarounds below. Community Edition is provided as-is and receives security fixes on its latest release only.

## Workarounds

Upgrading installs the protections; it does not switch on the SSRF mode. Addressing this class is a shared responsibility, and the network-layer measures apply to every deployment, including servers that have not yet been upgraded.

- **Upgrade to 2.45.1.** This is the first step, and the only one that adds in-product coverage of the outbound paths.
- **Filter the server's outbound egress.** Block the Portainer host's access to the cloud metadata address (`169.254.169.254`) and to internal ranges it has no legitimate reason to reach, and segment the server so its reach is limited to the Git servers, registries, Helm repositories and identity providers it must contact. This is the most effective single measure, and it applies regardless of patch level or edition.
- **Do not expose the Portainer API to untrusted networks.** Restrict access to internal networks or a VPN and place it behind a reverse proxy, per the deployment guidance. An SSRF vector is only as reachable as the account that triggers it and the network the server sits in.
- **Audit user access to the affected features.** Review who holds accounts at all, and limit the users and teams allowed to create or update Git-backed stacks and custom templates, manage registries, install Helm charts, and configure Helm repositories.
- **Consider the SSRF mode (Business Edition).** Deployers who want an in-product destination policy can run it in `Audit` to observe what their environment contacts, then move to `Enforce`. It is a complement to network egress control, not a replacement for it. Community Edition has no equivalent control; the network-layer measures above are the controls available to Community Edition operators.
- **Audit and rotate.** Review server logs for unexpected outbound requests, and rotate any cloud or registry credentials reachable from the Portainer host if compromise is suspected.

None of these replace the fix.

## Affected Code

The common root cause is that user-supplied URLs were validated only for syntax and then handed to an outbound client with no check on the resolved address. The shared validator illustrates the pattern:

```go
// pkg/validate/validate.go - IsURL
func IsURL(urlString string) bool {
  strTemp := urlString
  if !strings.Contains(urlString, "://") {
    strTemp = "http://" + urlString
  }
  u, err := url.Parse(strTemp)
  return err == nil && u.Host != ""
}
```

The fix introduces a centralized SSRF package. At its core is a safe dialer that resolves the destination hostname, checks every resolved IP against the configured destination policy, and then dials the already-resolved IP, closing the DNS-rebinding window between validation and connection. Redirects re-enter the same dialer. This dialer is wired into the global HTTP transport, the Git protocol handlers for `git`, `ssh`, `http` and `https` (with `file` disabled outright), the Helm repository and chart-resolution getters, the registry and ORAS clients, the GitLab and GitHub proxy clients, and the Azure Git client. Where a library builds its own HTTP transport rather than using the process-wide one, the corresponding path supplies the checked transport explicitly, and user-facing handlers additionally pre-flight the submitted URL. Static analysis rules reject new unchecked HTTP transports to prevent regressions. Outbound requests made by third-party libraries that manage their own network connections sit outside the HTTP transport this control wraps; the paths named in this advisory have been brought under it, and further paths are handled as hardening work as they are identified.

Coverage was completed in stages: the core mechanism and the majority of per-handler checks landed first, and the remaining library-owned paths - Git over HTTP/HTTPS, and Helm chart resolution and dependency download - were brought under the same dialer in 2.45.1.

## Impact

The outcomes below are ordered from most to least deployment-dependent. Their realism on a given install is governed by the operator's network posture - exposure, segmentation, egress filtering.

- **Cloud credential theft (highest impact, deployment-dependent).** Where the server has unrestricted reach to the instance metadata service (`169.254.169.254`), an attacker can, on the paths that return the response body, retrieve IAM credentials granting whatever the Portainer instance's role permits. Egress filtering or metadata-endpoint restriction removes this outcome.
- **Full-read access to internal services.** The GitLab proxy and several manifest and registry paths return the upstream response to the caller, turning the server into a read proxy for services on networks the user cannot otherwise reach - bounded by the server's own network reach.
- **OAuth bearer-token disclosure.** The admin-configured OAuth resource-URI fetch forwards an `Authorization: Bearer` token to the supplied URL.
- **Internal network reconnaissance.** On blind paths such as Git clone, Helm chart resolution and registry ping, differences in timing and error messages reveal which internal hosts and ports are live. These paths do not return the upstream response body and so do not yield metadata credentials.
- **Onward reach into managed systems.** Because Portainer is a control plane, internal access obtained here can extend to the environments it manages - again bounded by network segmentation.

- 2026-03-05: Reported via GitHub Security Advisory by **cwanglab** (templates URL, Kubernetes manifest URL, OAuth resource URI, registry ping).

- 2026-06-04: Reported via GitHub Security Advisory by **alcls01111** (Git repository file preview, including non-HTTP URL schemes).
- 2026-06-04: Dedicated hardening for the GitLab registry proxy vector released in 2.39.3 and 2.33.9.
- 2026-06-05: Reported via GitHub Security Advisory by **iaohkut-from-NightWolf-Team** (Helm repository search; registry ping).
- 2026-06-09: Centralized SSRF control merged to `develop`.

- 2026-06-19: Extended transport wrapping and additional per-handler checks merged to `develop` and to `release/2.43`.
- 2026-06-23: Reported via GitHub Security Advisory by **Shahid-BugB** (Git repository file preview, with upstream response reflected in the clone error).
- 2026-06-24: 2.43.0 released with the control.
- 2026-07-23: Duplicate report received via GitHub Security Advisory by **TristanInSec**; merged into this advisory with credit.
- 2026-07-30: 2.44.0 released, inheriting the control.
- 2026-08-13: 2.39.6-LTS released with the backported control.
- 2026-08-27: 2.39.7 and 2.45.0-LTS released.
- 2026-09-08: Duplicate report received via GitHub Security Advisory by **Reload3d**; merged into this advisory with credit.
- 2026-09-09: Internal source audit identified the remaining library-owned outbound paths.
- 2026-09-17: 2.39.8 and 2.45.1-LTS released; 2.45.1 completes coverage of the outbound paths.
- 2026-10-05: Duplicate report received via GitHub Security Advisory by **huynvi**; merged into this advisory with credit.
- 2026-10-08: Advisory published.
repo.summary: Server-Side Request Forgery across multiple outbound-request features
